meta.subtitle: Which visualization types to add next, why each one improves long-form reading, and how to implement each without breaking the no-build, single-file ethos.
meta.summary: Survey of visualization families the kit doesn't yet cover (heatmap, histogram, graph, treemap, sankey, radar, gauge, waffle, sparkline, calendar-heatmap, box-plot, slope, plus Mermaid-side ER / state / mindmap / timeline). Compares four implementation strategies, ranks candidates by reader value vs effort, and lands on a phased roadmap.

blocks.summary: The kit covers Cartesian and categorical comparison well. It does not yet cover density (heatmap, histogram), hierarchy (treemap), relational (graph, sankey), multi-axis (radar), progress (gauge, waffle), or inline trend (sparkline). Each gap has a documented reader use case in long-form replies — review summaries, design docs, architecture write-ups. The recommendation is a three-tier rollout: ship eight in-house SVG types first, unlock six existing Mermaid types behind the diagram primitive, and defer two lazy-CDN libraries until a concrete page asks for them.
bullets: Eight in-house SVG types ship first — heatmap, histogram, sparkline, calendar-heatmap, treemap, radar, gauge, waffle. All fit the existing chart kind via a new type value.
Six Mermaid types unlock for free — ER, state, class, mindmap, timeline, gitgraph. They're already in the Mermaid bundle the kit lazy-loads; the diagram primitive needs a doc update, not code.
Two heavy ones defer — graph (force-directed) needs d3-force lazy-loaded; sankey gets Mermaid's beta first and an in-house renderer only if a doc page requires layout control.

Cross-cutting floor — every new type needs title, source-note slot, toolbar (copy / screenshot / lightbox), light-dark tokens, viewBox-responsive sizing, and a data-table fallback under <details> for accessibility.

blocks.title: What's there today
blocks.lead: Two visualization primitives, with the type set frozen at their current state.

rows: in-house SVG with pan / zoom / log scale / PNG export
trends, correlations, two-axis distributions, market-position framing
in-house CSS bars with stats counter
flowchart, sequence, gantt, class, state (loosely documented)
Mermaid 10 lazy-loaded from CDN, themed from CSS tokens at boot and on theme toggle
process steps, request-response choreography, schedule view

blocks.summary: Mermaid is already on the page

content.content: Anything in this plan that says "already loaded" means Mermaid is already on the page when a diagram block is present. Unlocking a Mermaid sub-type costs zero bytes — only documentation and a sample in reference.json.

blocks.title: Gap inventory by data family
blocks.lead: What classes of visualization a long-form documentation reader expects that the kit can't currently render. Each family is the smallest set that justifies a separate type — sub-variants are noted but don't all need their own slot.

cards.title: Distribution
cards.content: Show how a single quantity is spread across a population. Today the only option is a bar with one bar per bucket — which works for 5-10 buckets and breaks down beyond that. No way to communicate density or quartiles.
items: **Histogram** — frequency by bin, the staple.
**Box plot / violin** — quartiles, outliers, distribution shape.
**Ridgeline** — many small distributions stacked, comparing groups.
**ECDF** — cumulative; technical readers prefer it over histograms for tail behaviour.

cards.title: Density (2D)
cards.content: Show a value across two categorical or binned axes. The cell-grid pattern is one of the most-requested visualizations in technical docs (correlation matrices, latency / load matrices, on-call heat).
items: **Heatmap** — N×M matrix of cells coloured by value.
**Calendar heatmap** — date-of-year × day-of-week grid; activity-over-time staple.
**Correlation matrix** — square heatmap with axis labels; specific shape of heatmap.

cards.title: Hierarchy
cards.content: Show parts of a whole that nest. Donut handles flat shares; nothing handles depth.
items: **Treemap** — nested rectangles, area-proportional. Composition + drilldown.
**Sunburst** — radial treemap. Niche; defer.
**Tree diagram** — node-link tree. Mermaid covers the simple case via flowchart with a tree layout.

cards.title: Relational / flow
cards.content: Show what connects to what, with optional flow magnitudes. Architecture, dependency, allocation, traffic-routing diagrams all live here.
items: **Graph (force-directed)** — nodes + edges, simulated layout.
**Sankey** — left-to-right flow with band widths proportional to magnitude.
**Chord** — circular relational; specialised, defer.
**Arc diagram** — nodes on a line with arcs; specialised, defer.

cards.title: Multi-axis comparison
cards.content: Compare entities across several dimensions at once. Bar groups force the reader to scan; radar collapses to one shape per entity.
items: **Radar / spider** — N axes, one polygon per entity. Best for 3-8 axes.
**Parallel coordinates** — many axes, one polyline per entity. Defer.

cards.title: Progress / status
cards.content: Show a value against a target, or a count as discrete units. KPI tiles cover the bare number; nothing renders the gap or the magnitude visually.
items: **Gauge / meter** — single value on a 0–max arc, with target tick.
**Bullet chart** — actual vs target on a horizontal track.
**Waffle / dot matrix** — 100-cell grid coloured by category, intuitive percentages.
**Funnel** — conversion stages; niche.

cards.title: Inline / micro
cards.content: Tiny charts that live next to or inside a prose run, KPI tile, or table cell. Today every chart is a block.
items: **Sparkline** — inline mini line / area trend.
**In-cell bar** — table-cell bar overlay; deferred until tables sprout the affordance.

cards.title: Temporal narrative
cards.content: Events on an axis. Gantt covers durations; events are a different shape (single point per item with grouping).
items: **Timeline** — events on a horizontal axis, grouped by track.
**Stream graph** — stacked area centred on a baseline; defer.

blocks.title: Design constraints — kit philosophy
blocks.lead: Before picking strategies, restate the rules every viz must obey. These are the constraints that rule out half the obvious solutions.

blocks.title: Non-negotiables
content: **No build step for content.** Authors write JSON; the browser renders. Anything that requires precompilation (D3 .vl.json transforms, build-time SVG generation) is out.

**Standalone single-file works.** dist/standalone embeds every kit asset inline. A type that depends on a network library at view time is acceptable only if the page is viewed online; otherwise it must degrade to the data-table fallback.
**JSON-authored.** The data shape is short, hand-writable, and validates against the schema. No bespoke DSLs that need a separate parser.
**Light / dark theme.** Colours come from CSS tokens, recomputed on theme toggle. Any library that hard-codes colours is wrong without a per-theme wrapper.
**Print-safe SVG.** viewBox-based, no clipping, text never hidden by transforms.

blocks.title: Numeric invariants per CLAUDE.md
content: Every viz must declare its layout invariants numerically: `boundingBox` dimensions, computed-style assertions for theme tokens, presence of the toolbar at a known position. "Looks right" is not a release criterion. A new chart type without a Playwright assertion sheet is not done.

blocks.title: Four implementation strategies
blocks.lead: Each new visualization can land via one of four pathways. Picking the right pathway is more decisive than picking the right type — a heatmap built four different ways takes 1×, 2×, 8×, and 20× the effort.

cards.title: A — In-house SVG renderer
cards.content: Pattern that already powers the nine chart types. New types extend the `type` enum and add a `_renderX` branch on the html-doc-chart Custom Element. Typical new renderer = 150–300 LoC.
items: Pros: zero CDN; single-file standalone works; theme tokens applied directly; toolbar / a11y free via the existing scaffold.
Pros: incremental — one type at a time, each one self-contained.
Cons: complex types (force-directed, sankey layout) take L-size effort.
Best for: heatmap, histogram, sparkline, calendar-heatmap, radar, gauge, waffle, slope, bullet, treemap, ridgeline, box-plot.

cards.title: B — Unlock latent Mermaid
cards.content: Mermaid 10 ships with ~14 diagram types. The kit currently exposes five in documentation. The rest are usable today by anyone who writes the correct first line of the source — but undocumented, so authors don't reach for them.
items: Pros: zero new code; pure documentation work. Highest reader-value-per-hour ratio in this plan.
Pros: theme already wired (Mermaid initialize is rebuilt on theme toggle).
Cons: Mermaid's visual language ≠ the kit's; some types (xychart-beta) clash with in-house chart styling. Choose the ones whose style is unique to Mermaid (relational / stateful).
Best for: ER, state, class, mindmap, timeline, journey, requirement, gitgraph, c4.

cards.title: C — Lazy CDN library, specialised
cards.content: When a single type genuinely demands a 100KB+ engine and in-house is L-effort or worse. The library loads only on pages that use the type, like Mermaid does.
items: Pros: matches the type's needs exactly; far less custom code.
Cons: supply-chain dependency; standalone single-file pages need an inline-or-degrade decision.
Cons: each library is a separate visual style to integrate with theme tokens.
Candidates: d3-force (force-directed graph), d3-sankey (sankey layout), cal-heatmap (calendar — but A handles this), vis-network (graph).

cards.title: D — One declarative engine for everything
cards.content: Vega-Lite (700KB) or ECharts (1MB+). JSON-authored, covers nearly every chart in this plan from one engine. Sounds like a fit for the kit; isn't.
items: Why rejected — bundle weight is incompatible with single-file standalone (the inlined kit balloons).
Why rejected — the engine's visual language is opinionated; matching kit theme tokens means an opaque options layer per type, eroding the win.
Why rejected — gives one renderer for nine more types; we get the same coverage from strategy A with twelve focused 200-line renderers and total kit growth under 2.5K LoC.
Reopen if — the kit pivots away from standalone single-file or grows past 30 chart types.

blocks.title: Candidate inventory — ranked
blocks.lead: Each candidate scored on reader value (how often a long-form doc benefits) × effort (size of the renderer or doc work) × strategy fit. The table is the planning artefact; the tier sections below expand the top picks.

rows: ER / state / class / mindmap / timeline / gitgraph
B then A — Mermaid sankey-beta now, in-house only if layout fights us

content.content: Effort sizes: S = 1–2 hours including tests and primitive entry; M = 4–8 hours; L = 1–2 days. "Reader value" is how often a long-form documentation page would reach for the type — high if every third page wants it, low if it's a once-a-year affordance.

blocks.title: Tier 1 — Ship next (eight types, one extension to chart)
blocks.lead: Each lands as a new value in chart.type, with its own payload shape. The renderer dispatches by type so unused fields stay ignored — same pattern as today. Each candidate below leads with an ASCII mockup of the rendered shape so reader can compare visually before reading the implementation notes.

blocks.content: Rectangular cells coloured by value. Optional row / column labels, optional value labels in each cell. Diverging palette for signed data, sequential for non-negative.

items: Shape: { type: "heatmap", rows: [...], cols: [...], values: [[v]], scale: "sequential"|"diverging" }.
Reader uses — correlation matrix, latency × time-of-day, error-rate × service, on-call coverage.
Implementation — SVG <rect> grid + computed colour via a token-driven palette function (light / dark already split).
Risk — palette accessibility; default to a colourblind-safe ramp (viridis / cividis) and document overrides.

blocks.content: Vertical bars per bin. Either pre-binned (author supplies bins + counts) or raw values + bin spec (kit bins for you).

items: Shape: { type: "histogram", bins?: [{lo,hi,count}], values?: [n], binCount?: 20, density?: false }.
Reader uses — illustrating a distribution claim in prose; one-axis variant of scatter.
Implementation — reuses the existing Cartesian SVG plot (axes, pan, zoom). Bar drawing is a four-line addition.
Risk — overlap with bar; document the distinction (categorical bar = labelled; histogram = binned numeric).

blocks.content: Inline mini line / area. No axes, optional endpoint dot, optional last-value label. Renders in line height; usable inside paragraphs, KPI tiles, table cells.

items: Shape: { type: "sparkline", values: [n], variant: "line"|"area"|"bar", showEndpoint?: true }.
Reader uses — trend hint without spending a block; KPI tile + sparkline reads as one composite.
Implementation — SVG with no axes, sized by parent font metrics; one of the smallest renderers.
Risk — inline rendering needs the inline-node pathway, not the block pathway. Decide schema location: extend the inline kinds or expose via a thin { kind: "sparkline" } block.

blocks.content: GitHub-style activity grid — date-of-year × day-of-week. One cell per day, coloured by value. Month labels along the top.

items: Shape: { type: "calendar-heatmap", year: 2026, values: { "2026-01-01": 4, ... }, scale?: "sequential" }.
Reader uses — ‘how active was X over the year’, incident frequency calendar, release cadence.
Implementation — date math + the heatmap renderer. Year auto-derives if all keys share one. Multi-year stacks vertically.
Risk — locale for week-start (Mon vs Sun) and month names. Default Mon-start; expose via meta.locale once it exists.

blocks.content: Nested rectangles, area proportional to value. Single level of depth ships first; recursive nesting deferred to a follow-up.

items: Shape: { type: "treemap", items: [{ label, value, color? }] } — flat first; children: [...] later.
Reader uses — composition (LoC by language, spend by category, traffic by route).
Implementation — squarified treemap layout (~80 LoC, no dep) + SVG rects + label placement (skip labels in cells smaller than a font-em).
Risk — label collision on small cells; tooltip on hover covers the gap.

blocks.content: N axes radiating from a centre; one filled polygon per entity. Best for 3–8 axes and 1–4 entities.

items: Shape: { type: "radar", axes: [{label, max?}], series: [{name, values: [n]}], scale: "shared"|"per-axis" }.
Reader uses — feature comparison across criteria; team-strength snapshot; tool-shortlist comparison.
Implementation — polygon points = (centre + r·cos / sin); axis ticks; legend reuses the bar-chart legend chip.
Risk — radar is notoriously misread when axes aren't independent or scales differ; document the per-axis scale option clearly.

blocks.content: Semicircular arc, 0 → max, with a needle / fill at the current value and an optional target tick.

items: Shape: { type: "gauge", value: n, min?: 0, max: n, target?: n, label?: "...", zones?: [{from,to,tone}] }.
Reader uses — single-metric status (SLO budget, runway, uptime) where the gap-to-target is the point.
Implementation — SVG arc paths + needle line + value text in the centre; ~120 LoC.
Risk — gauge is the most-criticised chart type in dataviz; restrict to single-value-vs-target framings only and document when bar / bullet is better.

blocks.content: 10×10 grid of cells (or N×M, configurable). Each cell = one unit; cells coloured by category. Intuitive percentages and counts.

items: Shape: { type: "waffle", total: 100, rows?: 10, cols?: 10, segments: [{label, count, color?}] }.
Reader uses — ‘40 of 100 users did X’; risk-portfolio; population breakdown.
Implementation — flex grid of <rect>s + legend (reuse bar-chart legend). Among the smallest renderers in this plan.
Risk — none material; pure layout.

blocks.title: Schema shape
blocks.content: Today the diagram schema only constrains source: string. After unlocking, document the supported first-line triggers as a free-form list, but keep the schema permissive — Mermaid evolves, and over-constraining the schema is the wrong place to enforce it. The kit's lint can grow an optional diagram-type warning later if confusion comes up.

blocks.content: box-plot · ridgeline · slope · bullet · funnel. All S-size in-house SVG. Each lands the same way Tier 1 does (new chart.type, dedicated renderer, regression test). Not a backlog item; ‘will not ship’ unless the listed reopen trigger fires.

blocks.title: Cross-cutting rules — every new viz
blocks.lead: Floor that every new type meets before it's considered done. Carry this list into each implementation PR.

items: **Title + caption slot** — both optional, but rendered in consistent positions (top + below the chart).
**Source-note slot** — optional `source` string under the chart, small-print, italic. Where the data came from.
**Toolbar** — copy data (as CSV via the existing `__htmldocVisualTools.copyTable` flow), screenshot PNG, lightbox open. Reuses the chart toolbar pattern, no new chrome.
**Theme tokens** — every fill / stroke pulls from CSS variables; no hex codes in the renderer. Recompute on theme toggle.
**viewBox-responsive** — fits parent width down to ~360px without overflow; never relies on fixed pixel widths.

**Data-table fallback** — `
Show data...
` rendered alongside or below the SVG. Screen-readers get the data; keyboard users can copy from the table directly.
**Aria label** — `role="img"` with `aria-label` summarising the chart in one sentence (e.g. "Heatmap of 12 services × 24 hours of the day").

**Numeric invariants** — at least three: title presence + position, toolbar presence + position, SVG `boundingBox` dimensions. Each lands as a Playwright assertion once the browser test surface is wired (see CLAUDE.md).
**Reference entry** — every new type adds a code-sample + live render pair to `docs/reference.json` under the visual section. No demo sibling pages.
**Regression test** — content-regression assertion that the type is allowed by the schema and rejected when misshaped.

blocks.title: Recommendation
blocks.lead: The shape of the next two weeks of work, if this plan is accepted.

blocks.title: Phase 1 — Unlock latent Mermaid (1 day)
content: Highest reader-value-per-hour. Touches only documentation: `reference.json` gains six new diagram examples (ER, state, class, mindmap, timeline, gitgraph); the diagram schema description names the supported first-line triggers. Zero kit code changes.

blocks.title: Phase 2 — Eight in-house SVG types, in priority order (1–2 weeks)
content: Heatmap → histogram → sparkline → calendar-heatmap → waffle → gauge → radar → treemap. Each lands as its own commit with: schema extension, renderer branch, primitive sample, regression test, browser-verified bounding-box assertion. Don't batch — see commit cadence rule.

blocks.title: Phase 3 — Defer the heavy types until a page asks
content: Force-directed graph and in-house sankey wait for a concrete request. The reopen trigger is documented above; revisit when it fires.

blocks.title: Open questions
blocks.lead: Things this plan doesn't decide. Each one should be answered before its block hits Phase 2.

items: **Sparkline location in the schema** — block-level (`{ kind: "sparkline", ... }`) is simpler; inline-level (`{ kind: "sparkline", ... }` inside paragraph content arrays) is more powerful but needs the inline-node pathway to grow. Likely answer: ship block-level first, add inline form when a real KPI tile demand surfaces.

**Heatmap colour scale defaults** — viridis (better perception) vs the kit's accent ramp (better visual cohesion). Likely answer: accent-derived sequential by default, expose `palette: "viridis"|"cividis"|"accent"`.
**Calendar-heatmap and locale** — week-start day, month-name language. Defer until the kit has a locale field; for now Monday-start + ISO month names.
**Mermaid version pinning** — currently `mermaid@10`. Some Tier 2 unlocks need ≥ 10.6 (timeline). Decide whether to pin minor or stay on major.
**Treemap recursion** — flat-only first or recursive from day one? Recommended: flat first, recursive in a follow-up; one schema field (`children`) makes the upgrade non-breaking.

**A11y data-table fallback default** — `<details>` closed (less visual noise) or open (data always visible)? Lean closed, with a content-regression test that the data-table exists and has the expected row count for every chart on every page.
